Katalog Berita (Halaman 53/57)

#908. ‘In moments of pain, football comes together’: Spain says goodbye to Jesús de Miguel

Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but the streets of Navahermosa were fuller yet quieter to mourn the Tenerife striker at his funeral

The narrow streets of Navahermosa in La Mancha were fuller than they have ever been on Thursday afternoon and quieter too. Silence accompanied the funeral cortege as its made way from the funeral home to the parish church of San Miguel Arcángel carrying Jesús de Miguel Alameda, “Demi”, the Tenerife striker who died after an on-field collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono three days earlier. Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but now they were joined by the game he loved. “We wanted to be close to his parents, his wife and daughter. In moments of pain, football comes together more than ever,” said Luis de la Fuente.

The Spain manager did not say much else; there was not much else he could say, not much anyone could. These have been dark, desperate days, days when it was impossible to assimilate what has happened, and there will be more. “We will get through this together but we will need help, professional help,” the Tenerife president, Felipe Miñambres, said.

The club’s majority shareholder, Rayco García, had cried as they left the building where De Miguel’s body had laid in Santa Cruz de Tenerife and he asked the striker’s teammates to be close to his widow Maria, when he had vowed they would for ever take care of his daughter, Clara.

Maria was in the stands with 16-month-old Clara in her arms when, in the 96th minute of Monday’s second division game, she saw her partner chase a ball up the pitch to the centre circle where Owono crashed into him. De Miguel’s father was watching it from the hotel Alameda in Navahermosa, where he goes for most games. His son’s football career had mostly been played not far from there and from the Leganés home where he had grown up – at Fuenlabrada, Inter Madrid, Unión Adarve and Navalcarnero, then Salamanca and Castellón – but now he was 1,000 miles away.

Medical staff rushed on to the pitch. Players stood, terrified, while for six minutes De Miguel was treated there. He was then taken on a stretcher to the ambulance waiting in the corner where, the club reported, they were able to re-establish a pulse. He was transferred to the Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz, where medics succeeded in getting him to breathe again. He remained in a critical condition but, with his body temperature lowered, he was stable, they said.

With De Miguel’s parents hurrying to find a flight to Santa Cruz, where García collected them, doctors told Tenerife there would be no news until the morning. But at 3am, there was another call to say his condition had deteriorated neurologically. At 8am, he passed away; Tenerife announced his passing at 8.31am. He was 30. The preliminary autopsy pointed to a trauma of the thorax: commotio cordis which can only occur upon impact within a 40-millisecond window in the cardiac cycle. A routine investigation was opened, the focus not just on Owono but the medical protocol applied.

Football is supposed to be a safe space, a refuge, an escape. All those lines about giving your life to the game are not supposed to be literal. This didn’t make sense. The images and the outcome shocked; the contradictory combination of the improbability and the plausibility of it all made it harder still to come to terms with: this couldn’t happen yet it could have happened to anyone. “I am the same age,” Raphinha, Barcelona’s captain, said. There is an everyman quality about De Miguel. He was also a partner, a father. “How we loved him,” García told Cadena Ser. “He was so humble, his feet on the ground.”

His teammate Javi Alonso said: “He was a worker, a footballing labourer. He was in the AFE, the players’ union, and helped me a lot. He was a great teammate and a good person, wonderful. He was always willing to help.”

He had begun in the academy at Leganés, a modest start to a career at modest clubs; real football. It hadn’t been easy and he had endured injuries too. He met Maria when he was playing for Navalcarnero in the third tier: she lived in one of the houses in front of the small, municipal ground with its astroturf pitch. It was not until he was 27 that he played “professionally”, always understood in Spain as referring to the first two divisions. He took his teams there too, twice winning promotion.

He never played in the top flight and played 40 games in the second division: he was not a star and was not rich. García vowed that his daughter would not want for anything. Fran Sol, a former Tenerife player, started a crowdfunding page for his family.

Almería said that their gate receipts when they play Tenerife would go to the family. During the funeral one of the eulogies noted that playing in segunda for Tenerife was his dream, finally fulfilled at 30: this wasn’t the end of his career; it was the start. When they won promotion, he told reporters: “When I started playing as a little kid, I never thought I would live all this.”

An interview he did with Ser Tenerife resurfaced this week in which he said: “Nothing in life is easy. There will be good moments and bad ones too; it is a path you have to walk. Making fans happy is what makes you proud; seeing people celebrate goals is the loveliest thing in football.”

Now they mourned him, desperately sad. Outside gate No 9 at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López, fans brought flowers and left candles. So too did the squad, standing in silence. The Spanish Federation cancelled all Copa del Rey games. The Champions League went ahead; Como’s Nico Paz, whose father played for Tenerife, held up a T-shirt in his honour. Messages came in from across the game; minutes’ silences were held. Las Palmas announced that they will wear their third kit this weekend, because it is blue and white, the same colour as their rivals’ shirt.

They would prefer not to play at all. The players’ union De Miguel was part of said it wanted to stop, that it had canvassed footballers and they agreed: they were not ready, their heads not right. But La Liga decided all games will go ahead except those involving Tenerife, Andorra and De Miguel’s former club Castellón – a decision they did not finally confirm until Thursday afternoon.

By then, De Miguel’s funeral had finished. His body was flown to the mainland on Wednesday, the decision made to hold the funeral in his parents’ village, although there will be an event at Tenerife’s stadium on Saturday, open to everyone. Tenerife’s players and staff boarded a charter at 7am on Thursday and then went to Navahermosa by bus, all of them. The presidents of the AFE, the federation and the league came; the presidents of Real Madrid and Atlético Madrid, too. Representatives from clubs across Spain. Andorra’s owner, Gerard Piqué; president, Ferran Vilaseca, and general manager, Jaume Nogués.

The minister of sport, Milagros Tolón Jaime. Pablo Blanco, ambassador of Sevilla, the club that lost Antonio Puerta and José Antonio Reyes. Their midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili, a former teammate, who had asked for leave; the head coach, Luis García, said: “We’re people above all else.”

Before the cortege set off, Manuel Hernandez, De Miguel’s agent, said: “In those difficult moments, we want to thank everyone from the bottom of our hearts for the words and gestures, all the support we have received. We’re very grateful; to feel so much affection towards Jesús and see the impact he made on people is something we will always take with us. Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill but also leaves everyone who was fortunate enough to share their life with him great memories.”

Wreaths of flowers from all the clubs he had graced in his career covered the hearse as it edged towards the church, following the cross-bearer there, slowly and in silence. There was not enough room in the church for all those who were there. When they eventually came out on to the plaza again, Tenerife’s players lifted the coffin on to their shoulders and carried their teammate back through the crowd to his final resting place in Navahermosa.

Liverpool are planning their long-term future in goal, with the Brighton stopper linked

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool are looking to Bart Verbruggen of Brighton & Hove Albion as their successor in goal to Alisson.

Verbruggen has been in spectacular form for the high-flying Seagulls this season, keeping seven clean sheets in 10 Premier League appearances, with the Sussex outfit finding themselves second in the table – four points ahead of Liverpool.

Such good form means increased interest in some of Brighton's top performers, however, with the Reds turning attentions to the Amex.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is out of contract at the end of the season, with his imperiously high level having perhaps dropped this season with age.

The Brazilian is now 34 and has made a couple of high-profile errors this season – while his comments admitting that he missed Liverpool matches last season “to prepare for the World Cup” have not gone down well with fans.

Now, TEAMtalk have revealed in a report that the Merseysiders have begun to look to the future between the sticks and have identified Verbruggen as a “credible candidate who could provide stability and quality” in taking the No.1 shirt at Anfield.

Alisson was a transformational signing for previous manager Jurgen Klopp in the wake of Loris Karius' two mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final, establishing himself as arguably the best goalkeeper in the Premier League since joining the Reds from Roma on what was an all-time record for a keeper at the time.

Liverpool looked to future-proof the position in 2025 when they swooped for highly-rated Georgian, Giorgi Mamardashvili, but the 26-year-old has struggled to command the same kind of aura as Alisson.

Next summer, manager Andoni Iraola will welcome 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans from Belgian side Genk in a move that could rise to an impressive £30 million – but a need remains for a senior figure to replace their current first-choice in goal.

Verbruggen is said to be happy at Brighton, though there is interest in his services from Real Madrid, too, who are looking to life beyond Thibaut Courtois themselves.

Manager Fabian Hurzeler will not entertain offers for the Dutchman in January, according to the report, with the player himself reiterating that he is fully focused on life on the south coast.

“I don’t know what will happen in the future: no one knows,” Verbruggen stated recently, adding, “All I know is that, at the moment, I’m very happy in Brighton.”

#905. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous

It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town said they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an issue that leaves people scratching their heads.

This season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

The mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

The chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He says the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

“People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner says. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”

The Football Association says the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop new policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most important area of football policing that we’re focused on,” says Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”

Ankers says he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”

The Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, said one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

#903. Dalot’s muddled performances are just another symptom of Old Trafford chaos | Will Unwin

The stand-in left-back has become a pantomime villain but United fans are understandably struggling to focus their ire

Sporting success is, supposedly, a nigh-on irrelevance to Manchester United’s global brand. The money will stream in regardless thanks to the behemoth company it has become, leaving behind its football club roots and becoming the world’s greatest soap opera creating the sort of drama of which Phil Mitchell can only dream.

There is a strong cast of characters from the hated billionaire owners to the under‑pressure manager and pantomime villain Diogo Dalot, and a collection of storylines that are becoming hard to believe. Amid the supervillains, there are the unmistakable petty culprits who have brought United down to 18th place in the Premier League and Michael Carrick wondering how much longer he can survive.

Within four minutes, United were two goals behind and wondering if they could perform another miracle as they did against Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday. Compared with the start of the season, there is more fight and anger in this team, inspired by Matheus Cunha, a player who can match talent with desire. It was a fine collective performance from conceding the second until the break, admittedly with Dalot being caught out to allow Alysson through on goal, only to nudge wide on the verge of half‑time.

Dalot is part of the problem, an unwitting victim of circumstances, mainly that he is a disappointing right‑back being forced to play out of position because no one saw fit to find a backup for the injury‑prone Luke Shaw at left‑back. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, was targeted by supporters’ chants, suggesting that he leave the club with rather fruity language because he is a key reason that Dalot is bumbling along in a defence that has conceded 30 goals already in all competitions – the joint-most of any side in Europe’s top five leagues.

The Portugal international has been at Old Trafford for more than eight years but it is an overstayed welcome because he is not good enough. Every match involves him committing more and more petty footballing crimes that are adding up to a long charge sheet for someone who claims to be an experienced defender. He is so often found out of position, a first-time observer could think he is playing left-wing or central midfield.

Against Roma he was at least partly culpable for the Italian side’s two goals because he had lost his bearings. United got away with it that night and were given the chance to rectify the tactics and Dalot’s understanding of what a full-back should do, instead of acting as a catalyst for chaos that United could do without. Within a minute, however, he was confused about whether to go towards Alysson on the edge of the box or leave the Brazilian to his own devices. He chose the latter option, allowing the winger to get a shot away and through Senne Lammens’ legs for another dreadful mistake.

The 20-year-old Alysson arrived in the country in January but already looks a settled Premier League talent, and had the better of Dalot for the entire time the two were on the pitch.

Getting to 2-2 was an achievement and United were in the ascendancy but returned without Harry Maguire for the second half, putting greater responsibility on the shoulders of Dalot, who now had Ayden Heaven beside him. Dalot has 40 caps for one of Europe’s best national teams but none of that was evident when he tripped Alysson inside the box, allowing John McGinn to swing the momentum in Villa’s favour.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Dalot lasted until the 66th minute when Carrick had seen enough, getting his ejection held aloft in red. At least with the new rules, Dalot was forced to jog off within 10 seconds to speed up his exit after a disastrous day’s work. The United fans cheered when it was clear he was being substituted, preferring Patrick Dorgu. It was a rather underwhelming changing of the guard but everyone has had enough of the Red Devil they know.

Elsewhere, Dalot’s form would have led to him being dropped for repeated poor performances but United do not possess serious squad depth. They have won once in 10 league matches to leave them deservedly in the relegation zone after more than a quarter of the season. Dalot is a symptom of United’s chronic problems, with the simple truth that despite the results being appalling, no one on the bench, apart from the teenager Shea Lacey, is challenging for a starting berth.

No one likes to see an individual be the focal point of criticism for tens of thousands, especially as Dalot is merely a scapegoat. He shouldn’t be at left‑back or still even at the club because he has shown himself to be below par for far too long but there is a lack of cut-throat behaviour to rid themselves of the ineffectual. Without Dalot’s ineptitude, life this week would have been considerably easier for United. Of course, there were celebrations at full time after another dramatic comeback but it was not a win on any level.

#901. Lens were humiliated by Como. The pain continued against Marseille

Pierre Sage led Lens to second and glory in the Coupe de France last season. A lot has changed in the last six months

The Lens striker, Florian Sotoca, was completely motionless as he looked into the middle space from the bench. The game, finely poised at 2-1 with a few minutes remaining, was not beyond his side, but that is not the story his troubled face told.

Marseille had just restored their lead thanks to a goal from substitute Keyliane Abdallah. Bruno Génésio’s men would go on to take all three points and continue their unlikely charge up the table, but the atmosphere at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis was morose before Marseille had even stepped on the pitch. The match did little to lift the mood at the end of a week in which Lens made unwanted history.

A pre-match banner unfurled by Lens fans that called the players a “disgrace” had not even been put away when a miscommunication between Jonathan Gradit and Samson Baidoo gifted Marseille the lead after 82 seconds. The former’s pass dribbled towards the goalline and was tapped in by Amine Gouiri from just a yard out.

It was a disastrous start for Lens, who recorded the joint-heaviest defeat in Champions League history last week. The 9-1 thrashing by Como was also the heaviest home loss in the competition’s history. Yannick Cahuzac, the Lens manager, called it a “humiliation”. The club’s president, Joseph Oughourlian, scrawled the words: “never again” inside the dressing room. Losing to Marseille on Sunday was not as chastening but the defeat posed more questions about the club’s recent decisions.

When Cahuzac, a friend of sporting director Jean-Louis Leca, stepped up from his assistant role in September to replace Dino Toppmöller, who lasted just six games, there were accusations of cronyism. Cahuzac’s stint so far has been a poor advert for the practice.

After three defeats in the league, winless in the Champions League, a derby defeat to Lille, a record-breaking loss to Como, and the wheels have well and truly come off at Lens; the jury is out on whether Cahuzac can set them back in motion. It was one of his former teammates, Florian Thauvin, who equalised for Lens against Marseille – his former club – with a close-range header. The playmaker, a harsh omission from Zinedine Zidane’s latest France squad, has been a rare bright spot in an increasingly gloomy situation.

Génésio said earlier in the season that these were the kinds of games Marseille could compete in but not win. But, as the French maxim goes, “le foot va vite” (football moves quickly). The tide has turned in Marseille; five league wins in a row have taken Marseille from the relegation zone to the Champions League places.

Génésio says his team’s fragile revival exists on “a knife’s edge”, however recent results – including a win at Bayer Leverkusen in the Europa League last week – have fed into growing optimism that his limited squad (both in quality and quantity) might avoid the abject season that fans had assumed was inevitable. The achievement belongs to Génésio, as does this win, secured by substitute Abdallah.

The academy product was banished to the reserves after his performance against Le Havre last month. Génésio criticised “a kind of lobbying around the young players” (from whom he did not specify) and held firm on his stance. He got the desired response. Re-integrated, Abdallah popped up at the back post to give Marseille a win that has taken them up to fourth in the table. They were second from bottom before the last international break.

Lens have replaced Marseille as France’s crisis club. After the match the home players did a tour of the pitch, applauding the fans for their support. In response, the fans unfurled a banner that read: “Shame on you.” Le foot va vite. Just six months ago fans packed into the Bollaert in the wee hours of the morning to welcome home their heroes after they had won the Coupe de France final. That feels like a lifetime ago for the players, fans and Pierre Sage, the manager who delivered that trophy.

“We are sick,” admitted Cahuzac after the match. There has been soul-searching but also plenty of finger pointing. Cahuzac says he “isn’t worried” about his job. Despite the growing pressure, he certainly has reasons to feel reassured but his friend, Léca, is also under a bit of fire after a second summer transfer window considerably less successful than his first. Jean-Clair Todibo, Thorgan Hazard and Franjo Ivanovic all arrived with high expectations but have fallen way short of them.

The fans had a banner for Léca, too, calling out his “shit interview” after the defeat to Como. They wanted an “apology”. They did not get one but it is certainly a sorry state of affairs at Lens.

Monaco won their third game in a row in the Conference League last week, but their 1-1 draw at Le Mans was their fifth straight game without a win in Ligue 1. Filipe Luís says they need to “cleanse the minds” over the international break. When Monaco last won in Ligue 1 – against Lens in September – they were top of the table. They now sit seventh. The goals have dried up for Paris Brunner, Folarin Balogun – returning from injury – has yet to replicate the form that attracted Premier League interest and Matthis Abline put in an anonymous display against Le Mans. Monaco were reliant on a defensive blunder to open the scoring through Mamadou Coulibaly, who could be in trouble for a throat-slit celebration. Brunner was punished for a similar celebration earlier this season, although on that occasion it was directed towards the opposition fans. Le Mans, who equalised in the 90th minute through Erwan Colas, are also without a league win since September, but there was a strong show of support for manager Patrick Videira from the home fans, who also took a dig at the club’s unpopular football adviser Bruno Cheyrou. He evidently would not have popular support if he were to instigate a managerial change.

From cleansing minds at Monaco to exorcising demons at Nice. The club endured a shocking 2025-26 campaign, during which the relationship between fans, the players, and the club reached breaking point. It ended with Nice narrowly avoiding relegation to Ligue 2, thanks to a playoff win over Saint-Étienne. A new manager, Olivier Pantaloni, and a new sporting director, Roger Ricort, came in over the summer, but the players and Pantaloni continued to speak of the scars of the previous campaign. They showed in the opening four games, none of which Le Gym managed to win. Since then, however, only PSG have taken more points. Nice’s 2-0 win at Angers means they have picked up 15 points from their last possible 18. The club are now in European contention. Pantaloni is once again working his magic, just as he did at Lorient last season.

#899. 'Tinkerman' Alonso's Chelsea side still searching for identity

Struggling Sunderland get a narrow win at home against Chelsea

Constant changes in formation and personnel - and another disappointing defeat.

Xabi Alonso's frustration was obvious as Chelsea's struggles for identity continued in the 1-0 defeat by Sunderland.

It is starting to feel as though the Spaniard is the latest "Tinkerman" at Stamford Bridge, a moniker first associated with Blues boss Claudio Ranieri back in 2002-03.

For the first time this season, Chelsea lined up with a three-man midfield - but they were also without a recognised striker for the second match in a row, with Pedro Neto again struggling to lead the line in their loss at the Stadium of Light.

By contrast, struggling Sunderland were led by target man Brian Brobbey, who won a 36th-minute penalty after being brought down by Levi Colwill. Enzo le Fee converted the game's only goal from the spot.

That decision came moments after Chelsea were denied a penalty when Cole Palmer went down under a challenge from Luke O'Nien, but the video assistant referee ruled that contact had started outside the box.

Those two incidents in quick succession meant Alonso and his coaching staff appeared angry on the touchline after the Sunderland goal.

However, the Chelsea manager refused to criticise the officials after the game - instead he gave brief answers that changed the subject and were critical towards his players for not carrying out the gameplan properly.

Asked whether Brobbey was simply unstoppable, Alonso, 44, replied: "No, he's stoppable. He's stoppable, but we have to do it better than we did today.

"Out of almost nothing he got a couple of chances. He got the penalty as well.

"I'm not happy with how we defended that situation. It's something that we could have avoided, something that we had worked on during the week. To concede penalties is not good for us."

It left nowhere to hide for Colwill, who was substituted at half-time, with Moises Caicedo filling in at centre-back despite having barely completed a full training session all week and needing careful management of his own fitness issues.

Chelsea also created few clear chances, aside from a headed opportunity that Â£117m signing Morgan Rogers squandered, while Palmer also struggled - days after being left out of the England squad.

Before the season started, Alonso said he wanted his Chelsea side to be "unpredictable".

Although factors such as injuries are beyond his control, his side have achieved that, but to their own detriment.

Failed to deal with Brobbey - player ratings for Sunderland v Chelsea

Sunderland beat Chelsea for first league win since August

Chelsea have five wins, four losses and a draw in 10 Premier League games under Xabi Alonso

Only Tottenham (28) have made more more line-up changes than Chelsea (24) in the Premier League this season.

In the early part of the campaign, they at least had a settled and exciting front three of Joao Pedro, Rogers and Palmer.

It was largely the reason behind the positive start to the season despite failing to keep a clean sheet against top-flight opposition until Alonso's eighth game in charge.

With Caicedo injured, they suffered problems in midfield and continued to make changes from match to match, while also experimenting with personnel to fix the defence.

However, they largely looked on course to emulate the back-three system Alonso excelled with during his historic German double-winning season at Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24.

As Caicedo returned after the international break, however, captain Reece James was injured.

Joao Pedro featured in wins against Bournemouth and Everton before sustaining a thigh injury, having already missed Brazil's international matches.

Number one goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez broke his jaw in a collision at Everton, while Maxence Lacroix, who had been a near ever-present since joining from Crystal Palace in the summer, is expected to be out until January with a hamstring injury.

Defender Jorrel Hato has also suffered a setback in recent weeks.

It has left Alonso reacting to events when selecting his starting XI, with the Spaniard saying: "There are situations. Yesterday Josh [Acheampong] said he was not ready to play, so we are short of options and we need to walk through this step.

"Even when we win, when we lose, we miss some players that we have injured and for sure we are waiting for them to come back because they are important."

He admitted his side were missing Joao Pedro, although supporters have also been frustrated that Estevao Willian, who came on at half-time on Sunday, has started only one league match this season.

Prior to Sunday's game, Chelsea were averaging just 46% possession. They then dominated the ball at Sunderland (with 68.7% possession) but without creating many significant chances.

Meanwhile, only Crystal Palace have conceded more shots on target than Chelsea's 50, while the Blues top the league with 53 shots on target - meaning there have been plenty of chances at both ends during their matches.

Alonso can still be pleased with Chelsea having collected five more points than they managed from the equivalent fixtures last season, with the club on course to qualify for the Champions League while sitting fifth in the table.

However, that is a low bar after a dismal campaign last season, when Chelsea finished 10th.

Going into the November international break, Alonso remains a long way from establishing a style of play, or an identity capable of bringing consistency - although he promised promising in an interview last week that Chelsea would be "different" and "better" by the end of the season.

#898. Evanilson ignites eighth straight Bournemouth win at blundering Ipswich

Marco Rose paid tribute to his Bournemouth side after a hard‑fought 2-1 victory at Ipswich equalled the club’s record of eight consecutive wins.

Evanilson got the ball rolling after five minutes, scoring for a fifth successive Premier League match. With seven goals this season, he has already beaten his tally from the whole of last season.

His latest was a gift from the Ipswich goalkeeper, Christian Walton, who tried and failed to dribble past ­him in the area, and Bournemouth went two up after 27 seconds of the second half when Leif Davis could only deflect Ryan Christie’s strike into his own net.

Lewis Cook tripped Abdoul ­Ouattara in the area to provide the hosts with a lifeline and Jack Clarke scored the penalty with 17 minutes left to set up a grandstand finish at Portman Road.

However, Bournemouth stood firm to make it eight wins in a row and match the record set under Eddie Howe in 2012-13, a season which ended with promotion from League One.

Speaking after a win which came three days after a victorious journey to Sparta Prague, Rose said: “I am pleased with the first 70 minutes because we went two up and I didn’t feel like we struggled or can get any problems, but it’s [the] Premier League and one goal changed the momentum of the game.

“That is why I am much more pleased with the last 20 minutes. We suffered but we did it together.”

A slow start last month at Chelsea proved costly for Bournemouth, and even in last weekend’s 2-0 home win against Leeds the visitors had an effort ruled out after 11 minutes. That made goals at the start of each half particularly sweet for Rose.

“Last week I said we start slow and this week I said we start quite quick and score an early goal. I am a magician!” the German said with a smile. “No, we know we have to be ready in this league. We played Chelsea four weeks ago and we were two down after three minutes. That’s why we learned and always good to score an early goal.

“We were sharp, we were good and that’s what I really appreciate. I said before this week that it’s going to be really demanding for a team that is not used to have this kind of [­European] situation.”

Julio Enciso went close late on with two free‑kicks, but this defeat means Ipswich have only won one of their last seven in all competitions.

Gary O’Neil, their manager, said: “[We are] gutted with the result, firstly, because it’s what we are here for and probably performance-wise not much in it. To lose a football match you’ve not been outclassed in is hard to take. But if you give the ball to the opposition No 9 twice, it’s going to be difficult and that was the story of the game really.

“It’s the level so we have to find a way of not only being competitive in games, but can we now find a way to make sure these Hull [a 2-2 draw] and Bournemouth performances are four points and not one.”

#896. Where does Man Utd 4-4 Villa rank among best Premier League games?

Manchester United trailed Aston Villa by two goals after just three minutes and 40 seconds, the earliest they had ever been 2-0 down in the Premier League

When Manchester United and Aston Villa served up an eight-goal thriller at Old Trafford on Sunday afternoon, it was an instant Premier League classic.

While the match will not define either side's season, it will be remembered for years to come.

In fact, it was only the 29th time in Premier League history both teams had scored four goals each in the same match.

It was not the first time United have been involved in a high-scoring Premier League encounter, either.

Last December, the Red Devils had to settle for a share of the points against Bournemouth after another game where eight goals were shared.

And in Sir Alex Ferguson's final match in charge of United in May 2013, they drew 5-5 with West Brom at The Hawthorns.

But where does Sunday's match rank among the other remarkable matches we have witnessed down the years?

This result played a major factor in the outcome of the title race eventually won by Manchester United

Having blown a 10-point lead at the top of the table, Newcastle's title hopes suffered a major blow as they lost a classic in stoppage time at Anfield despite having led twice.

Sergio Aguero's late winner delivered the most dramatic end to a Premier League title race

In an extraordinary conclusion to the 2011-12 campaign, Manchester City scored twice in stoppage time to beat Queens Park Rangers on the final day and win their first title in 44 years.

Sergio Aguero's famous late winner ensured City pipped rivals Manchester United, who had already won that day, to the trophy on goal difference.

Andrey Arshavin enjoyed his finest night in an Arsenal shirt at Anfield

On another remarkable evening at Anfield, Arsenal's Andrey Arshavin produced a stunning individual display - netting all four goals for the Gunners to deliver a serious blow to Liverpool's title ambitions.

Zirkzee's goal was his first in the Premier League this season

United seemed dead and buried, not once but twice, as they trailed Europa League winners Aston Villa 2-0 and then 4-2 at Old Trafford.

But late strikes from substitutes Joshua Zirkzee and then Patrick Dorgu, deep into stoppage time, may have rescued not only a point, but Michael Carrick's job as United manager.

Cheick Tiote scored a sensational late equaliser for Newcastle

Arsenal were 4-0 up at and cruising at half-time as they looked to chase down league leaders Manchester United.

However, Abou Diaby was then sent off for the Gunners as Newcastle produced a stunning comeback to earn an improbable draw - with Cheick Tiote's thumping 87th-minute strike clinching the point.

Philippe Albert (right) scored a superb chip to round off Newcastle's 5-0 win

With Manchester United having beaten Newcastle to the title the previous season, this felt like payback for Kevin Keegan and his players, who had also suffered a 4-0 reverse to Sir Alex Ferguson's side at Wembley in the Charity Shield just weeks earlier.

David Beckham scored Manchester United's fifth goal

Manchester United staged a magnificent comeback from 3-0 down at the break to overwhelm Tottenham at White Hart Lane.

Dean Richards, Les Ferdinand and Christian Ziege all scored for the hosts but a transformed United hit back through Andy Cole, Laurent Blanc, Ruud van Nistelrooy, Juan Sebastian Veron and David Beckham.

Michael Owen provided the decisive moment for the hosts late on

Michael Owen's winner deep into stoppage time gave Manchester United a dramatic victory in a classic derby at Old Trafford.

The moment prompted Ferguson to set off on an impromptu wild dance along the touchline, while City boss Mark Hughes - whose side had come from behind three times - questioned why the game had gone on for six added minutes rather than the four allocated.

Mark Viduka scored all four goals for Leeds

Liverpool had gone 2-0 up early on with goals from Sami Hyypia and Christian Ziege, but Mark Viduka scored either side of half-time to drag Leeds level.

Vladimir Smicer restored Liverpool's advantage, before two goals in three minutes from former Celtic forward Viduka secured an incredible win for the hosts.

Crystal Palace's late show had huge implications in the title race

Title-chasing Liverpool had just lost to Chelsea at Anfield, but looked set to power themselves back into the race when they took a commanding 3-0 lead at Selhurst Park.

But they squandered that advantage in a chaotic final 11 minutes, leaving Luis Suarez in tears at the final whistle. Man City went on to win the league by two points.

This was another Arsenal v Manchester United match packed with incident

A tight pitch, a packed Highbury and another compelling contest between two of English football's heavyweights.

The Gunners went two goals up courtesy of Nicolas Anelka and Patrick Vieira only for the champions to draw level thanks to two Teddy Sheringham efforts.

But in a season when Arsene Wenger's side were to wrestle the title away from Manchester, David Platt scored the winner.

There were fireworks in the Highbury tunnel before play even got under way

Most people will remember this game because of the fiery exchange between captains Patrick Vieira and Roy Keane in the tunnel before the game, but the 90 minutes itself were just as thrilling.

Vieira opened the scoring for Arsenal before they were pegged back by an Ashley Cole own goal.

Another Gunners legend, Dennis Bergkamp, helped the hosts retake the lead before two goals from a young Cristiano Ronaldo and a delightful John O'Shea chip stunned Arsene Wenger's side.

Chelsea supporters enjoyed dashing the title hopes of their London rivals Tottenham

A match that meant most for a side that wasn't involved - the day that Leicester City were crowned champions will go down in footballing history.

Two first-half goals from Harry Kane and Heung-min Son gave Tottenham hope of chasing the Foxes down at the business end of the season.

But Gary Cahill and Eden Hazard scored to get Jamie Vardy and his Leicester team-mates' party started as tempers flared in the second half of a match dubbed the 'Battle of the Bridge'.

Eli Junior Kroupi's goal rounded off a thrilling evening at Old Trafford

Manchester United and Bournemouth played out at a Premier League classic at Old Trafford last season.

The hosts led three times and thought they had won the game when they scored twice in 129 seconds to turn a 3-2 deficit into a 4-3 advantage.

But Eli Junior Kroupi's strike in the 84th minute pegged Ruben Amorim's side back once again as both sides had to settle for a share of the spoils.

#895. Sabalenka starts pursuit of WTA Finals title with opening win

Aryna Sabalenka won her Group 2 opener against Karolina Muchova 7-6 (7-2) 7-5, while Mirra Andreeva made light work of Elina Svitolina in a 6-4 6-0 triumph; watch the WTA Finals from Indian Wells this week, live on Sky Sports Tennis

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Aryna Sabalenka got off to a winning start at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells, battling past Karolina Muchova 7-6 (7-2) 7-5, while Mirra Andreeva was also victorious in her Group 2 opener on Monday.

A two-time beaten finalist in the WTA Finals - including going down last year to Elena Rybakina, who stole her No 1 ranking this season - Sabalenka is looking to win the tournament for the first time.

Rybakina's late withdrawal due to a viral illness and fatigue aids Sabalenka's hopes, as does her opening victory over Wimbledon finalist Muchova, who made her sweat for it in a hugely-absorbing contest that ran six minutes shy of two hours.

Sabalenka was first to blink on serve in the first set, Muchova breaking for a 3-2 advantage, and again to lead 5-4, only for her opponent to break back immediately on both occasions - the second time when the Czech world No 7 was serving to take the opener.

Sabalenka then spurned a couple of set points in Muchova's next service game, but dominated the resulting tiebreaker, dropping just two points.

The second set followed a similar pattern to the first, though it was Sabalenka this time who was twice pegged back from going a break to the good, before the four-time Grand Slam champion claimed the decisive break of serve to lead 6-5 before serving things out and clinching victory on her second match point.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It was a tough battle, it's always tough matches against her," Sabalenka told Sky Sports afterwards. "She's such a high IQ player and every time you have to be focussed, ready for everything and have to play smart.

"I'm super happy I was able to start with a win."

World No 3 Andreeva, who won her first Grand Slam at the French Open earlier this year, enjoyed a much more routine win to start her tournament as she eased past Elina Svitolina 6-4 6-0.

It was a near faultless performance from the 19-year-old as she wrapped up victory in 71 minutes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

After saving a break point in her second service game, Svitolina couldn't hold off Andreeva in her next as she earned three more at 0-40 - converting the first for a 3-2 advantage she would not relinquish.

The second set was even more straightforward as Andreeva didn't drop a single game against the world No 6, albeit she did have to stave off four break points when serving the match out.

Much attention is focused on Andreeva this week after Jessica Pegula labelled her a "diva" who "needs to be humbled" during a conversation with her coach that was picked up on a hot mic in a practice session at Indian Wells.

The WTA apologised for failing to properly inform players about active microphones, with chair Valerie Camillo saying there was "a lack of advanced notice and clear signage" as she confirmed audio will now be switched off for practice sessions.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Andreeva said she struggled on court despite the impressive nature of her opening win: "I don't remember myself being so nervous on the court," she said.

"I felt like my legs were shaking. It was extremely tough, so I'm super happy to get through the match.

"My main goal today was to try to block out all of the thoughts and the emotions, force myself to move like supersonic, but it felt completely the opposite - I felt like an elephant."

Andreeva added: "After this match, after feeling so many nerves, I think it's going to give me more confidence knowing I can get through."

Pegula is in Group 1, along with Coco Gauff, Linda Noskova and Martya Kostyuk, who all got their tournaments under way on Sunday, with Pegula beaten in her opening match against fellow American Gauff.

#893. Le Fée’s penalty stuns Chelsea and breathes life into defiant Sunderland

A lot can change in five‑and‑a‑half months, but as an early winter chill descended on Wearside last week – both meteorologically and ­metaphorically – Sunderland were determined that some things should remain the same. Just as they had beaten Chelsea on the final day of last season to ensure European qualification for the first time in 53 years, they did so again on Sunday to lift themselves off the bottom of the Premier League.

The Sunderland performance was certainly familiar to their head coach, Régis Le Bris – “the identity, the intensity, the togetherness, the way we managed the game” – on the way to three crucial points.

Ultimately a patched-up defence, ­without the injured Dan Ballard and the banned Omar Alderete, kept ­Chelsea at enough distance to allow Robin Roefs a tranquil ­afternoon amid the tumult. Chelsea may be ­developing into a ­chaotic must‑watch under Xabi Alonso but they were ­subdued here and have fallen out of the top four. “We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win,” Alonso said. “We lacked a bit of patience and creativity.”

Margins were paper-thin in a game decided by two first-half penalty calls, the first not awarded to Chelsea after Luke O’Nien’s clumsy challenge on Cole Palmer, deemed after video assistant referee consideration to be fractionally outside the area, and the second given to the hosts by Jarred Gillett after Levi Colwill brought down the ebullient Brian Brobbey; the defender argued, not without justification, that the Dutch striker had a handful of his shirt too but the award stood.

Alonso, as ever, made no excuses, ­focusing not on the officiating and more on how he was “not happy with how we defended that situation”. Enzo Le Fée had been equally unequi­vocal just beyond the half‑hour, sending Mike Penders the wrong way and dispatching into the goalkeeper’s bottom-right corner for the game’s only goal.

Europe may be a blessing for Sunderland but the full-time mood had been bleak after the latest alarming performance in the home defeat against Dinamo Zagreb on Thursday. It had felt like a season watershed and only the captain, Granit Xhaka, Thomas Meunier and Roefs survived the cull here. That the talismanic Xhaka, the subject of strong summer interest from his former coach Alonso, had his afternoon truncated by injury after less than three ­minutes, felt like yet more of the ill fortune dogging Sunderland.

There was no feeling sorry for themselves, though. With this the start of a challenging quartet of fixtures leading into the Tyne‑Wear derby next month, it felt like this match had to be attacked to prevent an early-season hiccup turning into a full mid‑season tangle with relegation trouble. And Chelsea were greeted with determination and ­aggression, with Xhaka’s withdrawal not ­blowing that plan off course. Two zesty ­incisions by Chemsdine Talbi in the opening quarter-hour, in his first ­Premier League start this season, caused Alonso’s men flutters, the first leading to a blocked Trai Hume shot and the second presenting Brobbey with a clear opening that he would have expected to convert.

The passion was there, the precision maybe less so. O’Nien’s challenge on Palmer elicited a penalty appeal that did not end up being costly after the VAR check and Morgan Rogers headed wide from a Marco Palestra cross, but Chelsea could not capitalise on any potential home nerves. If anyone was prone to belated Halloween frights it was the Blues, particularly at the hands of Brobbey, who led the line with enormous presence. He took on and beat the last man Wesley Fofana before steering his shot just too high, past Penders’ near post, and then won the penalty that led to Le Fée’s winner. “He is stoppable,” Alonso said, “but only when you defend better than we did.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Such was Chelsea’s bluntness in the first 45 that the coach opted for not just a substitution but a reshuffle at the break, with Estêvão replacing the injured Colwill, beefing up the attack with Moisés Caicedo slotting into the defence. Sunderland continued to fight tooth and nail in a game that threatened occasionally to bubble over. Meunier was booked for a late tackle on Caicedo and shortly afterwards Brobbey was cautioned for wrestling Roméo Lavia to the ground, a continuation of an ongoing feud between the pair. When he was substituted, spent, for the ­enduringly ­popular Wilson Isidor halfway through the second half Chelsea must have breathed a sigh of relief.

Estêvão made one burst through the middle on to a Rogers pass but Reinildo Mandava stepped across to snuff out the opportunity. Yet even with little possession Sunderland looked sharper. A ball broke for Isidor after Chelsea failed to clear Le Fée’s through ball, Penders saving and the rebound not breaking for the Frenchman before Pep Chavarría cleared.

As the last 10 minutes approached Alonso sent on Geovany Quenda for Chavarría, and the young winger finally conjured a goal attempt worthy of the description, fizzing a shot just wide of Roefs’s far post via deflection. Talbi, finishing as he started, pinged one just wide from distance on the break as the home side still looked more likely, even with a third of possession. Sunderland had rewarded their crowd’s vociferous faith.

#892. Fan injured after falling through hole in stand

Tromso's Romssa Arena, pictured before a Conference League game against Brighton in August, is 200 miles inside the Arctic Circle

A fan was taken to hospital after a number of Bodo/Glimt supporters fell through a hole in the away stand at Tromso.

The Norwegian top-flight match at Romssa Arena on Sunday was paused just before half-time after Bodo keeper Nikita Haikin called for the referee's attention.

Bodo/Glimt press officer Simen Pedersen told the Reuters news agency that "up to five people fell through the stands".

"We stood and bounced to a supporter song, then the floor gave way," Bodo supporter Andrine Moen told local newspaper Verdens Gang, as reported by Reuters.

"It cracked in two in the row in front of us. There were at least two people who fell through the floor, but we don't know how far they fell or how many fell in total."

The remaining Bodo supporters were moved into other parts of the ground before the match resumed.

The match at Tromso's stadium - the northernmost venue in Norway's Eliteserien - was played in heavy rain.

The score was 0-0 at the time of the incident, but Bodo forward Ola Brynhildsen scored twice after the game resumed to give the league leaders a 2-0 win.

Bodo are locked in a title battle with Viking and the Eliteserien season is set to finish in the first week of December.

#891. Michael Douglas’ Kids Dylan & Carys Support Him During Rare Appearance

Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones' kids Dylan Douglas, 26, and Carys Douglas, 23, helped honor their dad at the Art of Freedom Gala 2026 in New York City Nov. 4.

Michael Douglas was no solitary man during his latest outing.

The Basic Instinct actor was supported by his son Dylan, 26, and daughter Carys, 23—who he shares with wife Catherine Zeta-Jones—as he was honored at the Art of Freedom Gala 2026 Nov. 4.

Michael received a Lifetime Achievement Award by the Tibet House US at the event in New York, honoring his decades of peace activism and longtime role as a United Nations Messenger of Peace, a role he's held since 1998.

The 82-year-old sported a navy suit, posing alongside Dylan, who opted for a walnut-colored suit over a patterned shirt, and Carys, who wore a long-sleeved black top tucked into a tea-length khaki skirt adorned with an irregular pattern of sequins for the occasion.

After the event, Michael—who also shares son Cameron, 47, with ex-wife Diandra Luker—shared a photo of himself posing with his youngest children at the event.

"A wonderful night in NYC with @carys.douglas and @dylan__douglas," he wrote on Instagram. "Thank you to @tibethouse.us for honoring me with the Art of Freedom Award. Truly grateful for this special recognition and for such a memorable evening!"

And while Catherine wasn't able to attend the gala, their family's outing comes after the Wednesday actress recently opened up about what has made her and Michael's 26-year marriage last.

“Being kind to each other,” she told E! News last month. “And we have a very similar, sick, dry sense of humor. Which, in any circumstance that you find yourself in, within 28 years—we were two years together before we go married—you’ve got to find humor in it. It may not be funny at the time, but you got to look back at it and go, ‘You gotta laugh at that now, remember when that happened?’”

In addition to patience, the 57-year-old also cited giving one another “free reign” to pursue projects that appeal to them as a key to making their relationship work.

“He loves nothing more than when he sees the joy my acting brings me,” Catherine explained. “I don’t want to be away from him for seven months, coming back and forth, but we make it work. We always find those times and those long weekends where we can reconnect, and then off we go.”

#890. Szoboszlai a doubt for Nations League conclusion

Dominik Szoboszlai has made eight Premier League appearances for Liverpool this season

Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai will undergo tests on a knee injury to ascertain his fitness for Hungary's Nations League fixtures against Georgia and Northern Ireland.

The 26-year-old was replaced after 69 minutes of the Anfield club's 3-1 Premier League victory over Crystal Palace on Sunday.

The Hungarian Football Federation have said their captain is "following the usual protocol in such cases" and that they will offer an update on his availability as soon as possible.

Hungary are second in Nations League Group B2, one point behind leaders Northern Ireland who they play in the concluding fixture of the campaign in Budapest on 17 November.

Before that potential decider, Marco Rossi's side travel to Georgia on Saturday.

Speaking after the win over Palace that lifted the Reds up to fourth in the Premier League table, Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said he appreciates the player will do all he can to be available for his country.

"I know he will do everything to go because he loves to play with the national team, but he was not 100% when he finished the game.

"I suppose they will have to analyse, the medical staff, and see what it is.

"I know what I want, but I also have to understand the national teams. I'm sure that Dom, if he is fine he will want to go, but I'm not sure if he's going to be fine."

Szoboszlai, along with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo, missed Liverpool's 3-0 defeat by Manchester City in October directly following a four-game international window with Iraola keen to avoid any further stress on his playing squad.

"The last thing we need now is to lose players in the international games," he said.

"Last time, in the international break, we lost three very important players, so now I'm praying â it's the last thing we need.

"I think [Szoboszlai] extended a little bit the knee, it was fine, but not 100%, so he has to be careful to see if he can play with the national team or not."

#889. Diego Gómez hits another stunner as Brighton beat 10-man Brentford to go second

Who can stop Brighton’s ­ascension in English and European football? They are setting standards, ­practices ­leaving almost everybody else ­trailing in their wake. A ­second‑place position in the ­Premier League would once have read like a glitch in a ­Football ­Manager ­session. Not in November 2026, where they appear the only team capable of throwing down any sort of challenge to Arsenal.

Under low winter sun, Brentford, an opposition to which Brighton are often, if lazily, compared, were ­swatted aside. If Keith Andrews’s team, and their fans at the Amex ­Stadium, could level blame at a couple of ­refereeing decisions, they received little chance of rescuing anything. Brighton squeezed them, toyed with them.

If Pascal Gross, scorer of a perfectly hit penalty, attempted to dampen expectations of a title challenge, his manager, Fabian Hürzeler, allowed fans to dream. “They should always be excited, it’s our job to make them excited,” he said.

A successful return to the Amex Stadium following five Brighton away trips, more than 5,000 miles on the road including victories at ­Manchester City and Getafe over the past two outings. Brentford returned to a stadium where they have never won in the Premier League. Normal service was duly resumed, any Brighton negatives coming in a failure to add to their first-half goals.

An up-and-under straight from the kick-off was a rare Brentford foray into the Brighton box. Bart Verburggen catching it on the full prefaced an easy afternoon for the Brighton goalkeeper. There are many further dimensions to ­Hürzeler’s team. Last week Paul Scholes, an unlikely ­progressive, declared himself an admirer of a “level of ­coaching” he suggested is ­unsurpassed in ­English football. “The one thing that is non‑negotiable is to always put the team first,” Hürzeler said.

Diego Gómez’s opener was not as spectacular as the halfway-line goal of the season against Crystal Palace but a beauty nonetheless. Caressing the ball first with his left and then with his right, he laid up a thrash past Caoimhín Kelleher. Its trajectory was unerring, unstoppable. Hürzeler revealed: “Yesterday, he changed to shooting with [his] left foot … I couldn’t see him scoring with his left foot. I asked him after where this quality came from.”

The path to a commanding win opened up. Igor Thiago did not last many ­minutes beyond his failed attempt to lob ­Verburggen. Scuffling in midfield with Chema Andrés, his shove was first ruled a yellow by the referee, Michael Oliver. In stepped the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell: “violent conduct” and “with force” was the verdict from Stockley Park.

Afterwards, Andrews was ­visibly unhappy: “We’ve lost two games and both when down to 10 men. So we need to analyse ourselves first. In both scenarios we can do better. In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation.”

Infact, both Yehor Yarmolyuk and Vitaly Janelt were dismissed against Liverpool, and if Andrews rues such lapses of discipline he was more unhappy at the initial decision’s video-assisted overturn: “The game is in a state now of a place I don’t particularly like.”

Straying beyond the confines of his technical area in a manner likely to add him to Mikel Arteta’s “massive storage of images” of such breaches, Andrews asked his team to dig deep but Brighton’s dominance of possession became near-total.

Luka Vuskovic, ­serving ­previously as a deep-lying playmaker, won the penalty. Keane Lewis-Potter’s ­panicked response to a physical 18-yard box mismatch was to snatch at the ­Croatian’s shirt. Gross’s penalty was struck as truly as Gómez’s goal. “We need to be cuter,” Andrews said. “I take real pride in the way we defend set pieces and we need to do better because that wasn’t good.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andrews’s half-time ­adjustments, bringing on Yarmolyuk and Nathan Collins, was an attempt to protect Brentford’s goal difference. Brighton continued to pile on pressure, their ­possession share reaching beyond 75%. A set piece became Brentford’s sole route back, though Mathias Jensen’s diagonal into ­Verbruggen’s hands would not have passed muster in rugby’s Nations Championship.

Ironic cheers from the away end came when Brentford won a corner, and then another – rare excitement at Brighton’s defenders being asked to do something other than build an attack. The visitors’ fighting spirit at least sustained, though threatened to spill over. When Kevin Schade shoved ­Vuskovic to the ground by the touchline, another red card was a possibility, only for Oliver and Attwell to rule a yellow as sufficient this time.

Brighton’s push for honours and further horizons will require more than spectacular goals. “You see the Premier League, the margins, you look at the results – we are not ­getting carried away yet,” Gross said. “Every game we have to suffer a lot.”

Hürzeler, like Andrews constantly straying beyond the confines of his technical area, does not countenance any let-ups. When Brighton meet the unstinting demands of their coach, so many are left in their wing mirrors.
