#809. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Admits to Having an Affair With Alleged Spy

Nvidia’s CEO, billionaire Jensen Huang, issued a statement admitting to an affair with a woman now suspected of being a Chinese spy: “I love our country and our company.”

Nvidia is powering advanced AI with a side of scandal.

In what sounds like a honey trap ripped straight from the pages of a James Bond novel, the tech company’s CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman the US government suspects to be a Chinese spy.

Yes, really. Jensen apologized for his actions in a message shared company-wide before being posted publicly.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he wrote in the Nov. 8 message, which did not name Alice. “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

While noting an apology can’t undo his actions, the 63-year-old—dad to two adult children—expressed hope he could earn back their trust over time.

The billionaire also addressed his Nvidia colleagues, noting standing at the helm of the AI infrastructure and gaming company has been the “privilege of my life.”

“My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he added to the Nvidia employees and stakeholders. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”

As for why the affair posed a national security risk, multiple outlets including The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that the woman Jensen had the affair with was Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese businesswoman the outlets said was recruited as a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

A personal familiar with the matter also confirmed to NBC News on Nov. 7 that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice was a Chinese spy and that she and Jensen had engaged in a relationship.

Alice, however, did not respond to The New York Times’ request for comment, nor has she issued a public statement. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun, meanwhile, said in a Nov. 9 statement, per The Associate Press, “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated,” calling such claims “nothing but smears.”

In his personal statement, Jensen noted that Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation, which was affirmed in a separate statement directly from the Board. Their statement also claimed the Board had no reason to believe that “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

As for his future at the company, it doesn’t look like Jensen will be left at a dead drop anytime soon.

As the Board of Directors statement noted, “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

Meanwhile, Jensen affirmed he supports the Board’s investigation and will “cooperate fully.”

“I love our country and our company,” he added. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

#808. Brady ends association with Birmingham City

Brady brought an end to his illustrious NFL career in 2023

NFL legend Tom Brady has ended his association with top-of-the-table Championship side Birmingham City.

The seven-time Super Bowl champion became a minority owner in the St Andrew's club in August 2023 when he "entered a partnership" with club owners Knighthead Capital Management LLC.

Part of Brady's role involved him being chairman of an advisory board at Birmingham, with the club saying he would be "both investing [as well as] committing his time and extensive expertise" following his arrival.

However, the Blues announced his exit, external with a statement headlined 'Tom Brady departure'.

They added: "Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.

"It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom's experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community."

Former quarterback Brady, a three-time NFL most valuable player, retired in February 2023 after 23 seasons in the NFL, having won six of his Super Bowl titles with the New England Patriots and one with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Following the end of his playing career, he also acquired a stake Las Vegas Raiders, while also becoming part of the ownership group of the WNBA's Las Vegas Aces.

On top of that, Brady's commitments also include him being a lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports.

He leaves with Birmingham top of the Championship on goal difference with 29 points after 15 games.

#807. Cameron Mathison Reveals "Incredible" New Relationship After Divorce

General Hospital star Cameron Mathison shared that he was surprised to find love with girlfriend Taelyr Robinson two years after he and ex-wife Vanessa Mathison split after 22 years of marriage.

Cameron Mathison has found his leading lady.

The All My Children alum revealed that he’s amazed to have found love with girlfriend Taelyr Robinson two years after he and ex-wife Vanessa Mathison announced their divorce in July 2024 after 22 years of marriage.

“Taelyr is just such an incredibly kind and sweet and smart and fun, adventurous and supportive and encouraging woman,” Mathison shared on the I Do, Part 2 podcast Nov. 7. “It’s just incredible.”

“We have tons in common,” he continued, “and I never really thought that I would have that much in common again with somebody after being with Vanessa for 22, 23 years.”

But finding love wasn’t so easy the second time around as the 57-year-old navigated dating apps.

And while he did meet “a lot of incredible amazing women,” he also realized that dating around was not for him and mostly served as a “distraction.” That is, until he met Robinson on the app Raya in April, going Instagram official in September.

“I met Taylor and obviously I am way, way better as a devoted, loyal, caring, loving partner,” Mathison said. “I was in a relationship for basically 25 years, including the time we were dating, so it was messy and odd and surreal at the time—55 year old was out on a dating app.”

For now, the General Hospital star is enjoying his romance with Robinson, explaining to podcast hosts Daisy Fuentes and Richard Marx that their relationship was still relatively new and he was doing his best to navigate some of the expectations.

“The Instagram official aspect, I’m usually more private and she’s younger than I am,” he noted. “But Instagram is a big deal and being Instagram official’s a big deal, I think more so to potentially younger generations. I’m learning and compromise and stuff, but I’m very open and happy to put it out there and share it with people.”

And Mathison—who is dad to kids Lucas, 23, and Leila, 20, with his ex—has clearly taken to sharing his love for Robinson on Instagram, sharing a sweet tribute for her birthday.

“Beautiful inside and out, and somehow even more so on the inside,” he posted Oct. 29 alongside a photo carousel of the two. “Happy birthday beauty. The world’s lucky to have you. And I am too :).”

For a deep dive into the love lives of more of your favorite soap stars, keep reading.

Kelly Ripa actually auditioned her future husband Mark Consuelos to play her boyfriend on All My Children.

"When I saw him, the photograph of him, I saw my entire future with him flash before [my eyes]. Like, I saw it," Ripa recalled to SiriusXM show "Lunch With Bruce" in August 2018. "I [didn't] believe in any of that and now I do because of that moment."

The couple eloped in 1996 only one year after meeting and are still going strong 25 years later. And the All My Children stars eventually had three children of their own, making AMC co-star Eva LaRue godmother to their eldest son Michael.

The All My Children lovebirds wed in 1996 and split in 2005. Yet Eva LaRue only had kind things to say about her ex John Callahan after his tragic death in 2020 following a stroke.

"My great friend, co parent partner, and loving father to Kaya," LaRue wrote on Instagram. "Love knows not its depth till the hour of separation. Our hearts are broken."

Before This Is Us, Justin Hartley was spending the Days of Our Lives with The Young and the Restless series regular Chrishell Strause. The couple dated for three years before tying the knot in 2016. While Strause went on to star in Netflix real estate reality series Selling Sunset, Hartley filed for divorce in 2019. They reached a private settlement by January 2021.

Hartley later sparked romance rumors with former The Young and the Restless co-star Sofia Pernas in May 2020; the couple quietly tied the knot in May 2021.

Daytime Emmy Award winner Eileen Davidson found love with co-star Vincent Van Patten in 2000. The only catch? They were both married to other people.

"We had a friendship for a long time," Davidson explained on The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills in 2016. "We just kind of fell in love. I told my husband at the time, ‘We have a situation here. I am having feelings for somebody.'"

Seems like it was the right decision because Davidson and Van Patten celebrated their 23rd wedding anniversary in 2026.

Before starring on Brooklyn Nine-Nine, Melissa Fumero and David Fumero connected on One Life to Live. They got married in 2007 and have two sons.

Jon Lindstrom married his As the Wold Turns co-star Cady McClain in 2014, although the couple announced their separation in 2024.

Courtney Hope was introduced to future husband Chad Duell through her General Hospital onscreen brother, Bryan Craig. The couple announced their engagement on Valentine's Day 2021. They married in September of that year, but split just two months later.

Kelly Thiebaud and her former General Hospital co-star Bryan Craig got engaged in June 2015 but went their separate ways a year later.

Bill Hayes and Susan Seaforth Hayes found a lifelong romance on the set of Days of Our Lives. They wed in 1974 and were together until his death in 2024.

Mick Cain certainly thought co-star Schae Harrison was Bold and Beautiful. The duo have been together for over 20 years since meeting on set.

As the World Turns stars Maura West and Scott DeFreitas got married in 2000, and are parents to four kids.

The Days of Our Lives former co-stars got married in 1996 and share son James Quentin together. Kassie DePaiva went public with her leukemia battle in 2016 and thanked her family for their support.

Doug Davidson began dating his Young and the Restless co-star Cindy Fisher in the early 1980s. The couple tied the knot in 1984 and have two kids together.

Technically Darin Brooks and Kelly Kruger fell in love as co-stars on sitcom Blue Mountain State but the couple did appear together on The Bold and the Beautiful. The couple were married in 2016 and welcomed their first child in 2019. They later split and finalized their divorce in 2026.

Casey Moss found true love with True O'Brien on Days of Our Lives in 2015. They married in 2025.

From playing a lovestruck couple onscreen to tying the knot off-screen, Days of Our Lives alums Crystal Chappell and Michael Sabatino wed in 1997 and have two sons together.

Art mimicked life as onscreen married couple Amelia Heinle and Thad Luckinbill tied the knot in real life. The couple called it quits after a decade of marriage in 2017, just as their The Young and the Restless alter-egos also had marriage woes.

The General Hospital duo got married in 2001 and are parents to four kids.

#806. Inside Brooklyn Pacha’s Opening Weekend: Exclusive Photos

The indoor club, which occupies the former Avant Gardner Great Hall, opened Nov. 6-7 with sets from Loco Dice, Louie Vega & more.

Six months after the opening of Pacha New York, the club’s indoor component has officially opened its doors to clubbers.

Brooklyn Pacha celebrated its official opening this past weekend (Nov. 6-7), with a Friday night lineup that included Loco Dice leading a bill that also featured Tiga and house artist HoneyLuv. On Saturday, the influential Nervous Records celebrated its 35th anniversary with a party featuring Louie Vega, Oscar G, Anané, Will Automagic of The Carry Nation and Victor Calderone.

See exclusive images of these parties below.

Brooklyn Pacha exists inside an 11,175-square-foot warehouse space that was formerly the Great Hall of the Avant Gardner entertainment complex. The complex was taken over by The Pacha Group in early 2026, with the open air Pacha New York opening in June and closing for the season on Oct. 31. Brooklyn Pacha will serve as a space for the fall and winter months, with the upcoming schedule including Miss Monique, Madeon, Luciano and many more into February.

“Brooklyn Pacha gives us a year-round home for the connection we saw on the dance floor during Pacha New York’s first summer,” Aloki Batra, CEO of FIVE Hospitality and The Pacha Group, tells Billboard. “We wanted to bring that energy into an indoor space with its own character, combining state-of-the-art d&b sound with lighting design by the team behind Berghain in Berlin. Every element serves the experience on the dance floor.“With Brooklyn Pacha through the winter and Pacha New York outdoors in the summer, we can develop a deeper relationship with the city and its music community,” Batra continues. “As Pacha approaches its 60th anniversary, this chapter is about carrying that heritage forward while earning our place in New York’s nightlife.”

#804. People don't know full story behind England exile - White

Ben White made his first England appearance in more than three years against Uruguay in March

Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the "full story" behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection - but says he would make the same decision again.

White, who has been named in Thomas Tuchel's squad for upcoming Nations League fixtures, left the Three Lions' camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to return home for personal reasons.

He then made himself unavailable for selection for the rest of Gareth Southgate's reign, and was booed by some fans in March's 1-1 draw with Ukraine after returning to the squad under Tuchel.

Asked by BBC Radio 5 live's football correspondent John Murray what he would say to people who define his England career by what happened in Qatar, White said: "I think obviously people don't know the full story, because I [have] never said anything and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

"It's been amazing [though], obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it is amazing to be here now."

White is now 29 and asked if he would have done anything differently in hindsight, he added: "No, I don't think I would.

"Obviously, I was a bit younger, I am a bit older now.

"I think as a person I am quite real and I think I made the decision that I would probably continue to make.

"So, one that I am not happy about, but obviously it happened and [it is] time to move on."

White came on for his first England appearance since 2022 in March's 1-1 draw with Uruguay and was booed by some supporters before he scored but also gave away the penalty that led to the visitors' equaliser.

After that, Chelsea midfielder Jordan Henderson said he and his fellow England players would always support White, while Tuchel said recently that the defender deserves "a new chapter" and "positive feedback from the crowd".

Asked how he dealt with the emotions of that night at Wembley, White added: "Before the game I was thinking 'don't not stand out, but [take it] nice and easy'.

"Then I came on and obviously got booed, then I scored, then I gave away a penalty.

"So, it was obviously full of emotions that night, [but] it was a good night."

England play Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before taking on world champions Spain in Madrid three days later.

White is looking to add to his six England caps in this international break and said: "It is obviously an amazing privilege to be called up.

"The feeling is the same every time you do get this chance to play for England. It's one I am really looking forward to this week."

#803. Kane and Bellingham air strong views in England World Cup review

Kane and Bellingham made their views clear at the review

England players are understood to have aired strong views about their World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in a team meeting.

As BBC Sport reported in September, the Football Association (FA) process included canvassing the opinions of the squad - and it has emerged that took place at a 'full and frank' meeting with head coach Thomas Tuchel at the start of the September international break.

BBC Sport has been told the squad feel that now they have been able to have their say, they can move on from their heartbreak in Atlanta on 15 July.

And this was demonstrated in the last international break when England, after a narrow defeat by Spain in the first game, went on to win the next three matches impressively.

Burn replaces injured Guehi in England squad

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feelings lingering and even growing throughout the summer.

In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.

Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.

As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.

Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.

Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.

Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.

It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.

There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.

That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.

There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.

All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.

As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.

Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.

Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.

If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.

Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too.

"It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week.

"I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."

We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.

#802. Why Guitarricadelafuente Said Yes to La Bola Negra Without a Script

Guitarricadelafuente explained the unconventional way he was cast in La Bola Negra and the emotions he felt writing the film’s original song “La Nieve.”

For Guitarricadelafuente, La Bola Negra was definitely his jam.

The Spanish singer-songwriter revealed how he went from making music to making movie magic in the drama, which is already an awards season frontrunner.

“The truth is that I said yes to this role a bit blindly because the script wasn't written yet,” Guitarricadelafuente told E! News in an exclusive interview, translated from Spanish, at the 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala Nov. 7. “There was only the idea of the character of Sebastián and for me it was like a gift from heaven to be able to participate in this film.”

Plus, the 29-year-old (real name Álvaro Lafuente Calvo) had good reason to trust his instincts. After all, he was already a longtime fan of the film’s co-writers and co-directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known as “Los Javis.”

“They knew they could count on me without me having the story in mind—they already knew I could do it,” he shared. “It was something that made me immediately say yes.”

Acting wasn’t the only way Guitarricadelafuente got to flex his creative muscles. He also wrote the original song “La Nieve” for the movie, though he admitted he “didn’t know where to begin.”

Ultimately, he found inspiration in the film’s focus on poet Federico García Lorca.

“The truth is that it was a beautiful journey to be inspired by all that poetry of Lorca that is so present throughout the film,” he explained, “and something to pay homage to all those lives that could not be possible in some way.”

Bringing Sebastián to life helped him find his voice, too.

“It came out as if I were able to experience the character in my own flesh,” he added, “and for all of that to come out in the most honest way possible.”

#801. Man Utd expected to sack head coach Carrick

Michael Carrick signed a two-year deal with Manchester United last summer

Manchester United look increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick.

The club opted to stick with Carrick after the side's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October, with the intention of reassessing the situation during this month's international break.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that the board remain committed to that process, and that no final decision on Carrick's future has been made.

However, there is a growing expectation that chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will recommend to minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family for Carrick to be sacked.

The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.

BBC Sport reported in October that the club had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann over replacing Carrick.

Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is known to be keen on the role, while multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford.

Pochettino signed an extension to his contract as USA coach in August.

However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.

Man Utd score twice in stoppage-time to share points in eight-goal thriller

The Villa draw was Carrick's third match in charge since the club opted to give the 45-year-old more time at Old Trafford.

Results during that time - a win, a draw and a defeat - were mixed, and displayed the best and worst of Carrick's reign with United shipping goals but displaying good character to come back from two goals down on three occasions.

United's board toyed with sacking Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth, but decided the Englishman - and his players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around.

It was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.

Unfortunately for Carrick, it makes for poor reading.

With one victory in 10 Premier League matches, United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986/87 season.

They sit 18th in the table, one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace.

Only the Eagles and Ipswich have conceded more than the 19 goals United have shipped in the Premier League this season.

It is hard to believe given the club's current predicament just how quickly Carrick's tenure has soured.

Four 'huge mistakes' that show Man Utd's defensive problems

Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.

With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.

Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Bruno Fernandes likes to occupy.

It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.

In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft later claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous".

"It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.

The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser.

The Portugal playmaker, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.

He has scored just once - a penalty against Villa on Sunday - in the league since.

After the Ipswich win came a trip to Everton.

Twice United led, the second occasion when Sesko struck two minutes from full-time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.

Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."

Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before their rivals benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.

Carrick's complaints were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.

After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.

The fine margins United benefited from during Carrick's interim spell were now going against them, and his coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.

Carrick called Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom of the table a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.

The whirlwind was starting to pick up strength.

Lisandro Martinez, who scored an own goal against Fulham, was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.

The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.

By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back that eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role was in full swing.

After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 Champions League defeat for United. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.

He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea. United were beaten in both matches.

With just three wins in 15 matches in all competitions this season and United stuck in 18th in the Premier League, Carrick is set to pay the price.

#800. Every Role Cast in the Snoop Dogg Biopic So Far, From Dr. Dre & 2Pac to Snoop Himself

'Snoop' hits U.S. theaters on Aug. 6, 2027.

Snoop Dogg is the latest rapper to bring his life story to Hollywood. The hip-hop legend broke the news that production was already in motion in April  on a biopic simply titled Snoop while speaking at CinemaCon in Las Vegas, and the Universal Pictures film is slated to hit theaters across the U.S. on Aug. 6, 2027.

The biopic will be directed by Hustle & Flow‘s Craig Brewer, while 8 Mile producer Brian Grazer is set to produce the film alongside the West Coast rap legend.

“After my brothers told their story in Straight Outta Compton, it’s my turn,” Snoop said at CinemaCon in reference to N.W.A’s 2015 biopic. “[Brewer] just showed us how hard it is out here for a pimp from Hustle & Flow. And then last year, he got us all singing ‘Sweet Caroline,'” he added of Brewer’s 2025 film Song Sung Blue.

Fellow rap deities like 2Pac, The Notorious B.I.G., Eminem, N.W.A and 50 Cent have all had movies made at least loosely about their life stories, and now it’s Snoop’s turn to hit the silver screen.

Snoop is still releasing new music more than 30 years into his career and he’s completed unfamothable side missions, like being a correspondent for the Olympics and co-hosting a cooking show with Martha Stewart.

The Snoop movie has already started to make casting announcements, with roles carved out for 2Pac, Dr. Dre, Suge Knight and Warren G, all of whom played a significant role in Snoop’s music career, as well as Snoop himself.

Find the entire cast for Snoop (so far) below. (This list will be updated.)

Once upon a time, Nipsey Hussle was offered the role of Snoop Dogg in Straight Outta Compton, which ultimately went to LaKeith Stanfield. Now, Outer Banks star Jonathan Daviss — also known as JD — gets his chance to play the Death Row legend.

The story of Snoop can’t be properly told without Dr. Dre, who became his signature collaborator, as they made magic on tracks like “Nuthin’ But a G Thang” and “Still D.R.E.” BMF star Myles Bullock will play Dre.

Lauren London will play Snoop’s mother, Beverly Tate, in the biopic. She has history with Snoop, as the ATL star appeared in the music video for 2004’s “Drop It Like It’s Hot.”

2Pac and Snoop Dogg became close friends in the ’90s as faces of Death Row Records while dominating the rap game.

Warren G and Snoop Dogg grew up as childhood friends in Long Beach, and Warren also helped Snoop get discovered by Dr. Dre. Algee Smith — who previously portrayed Ralph Tresvant in BET’s The New Edition Story — will play Warren.

Suge Knight is the co-founder of Death Row Records and brought Snoop into the fold of the scorching-hot label in 1992. Knight’s currently serving a 28-year sentence after pleading no contest to voluntary manslaughter charges in a fatal 2015 hit-and-run. Tre Hale, who plays Andy on the Apple TV+ series Platonic, will play Suge.

Shante Broadus is Snoop Dogg’s wife. The couple tied the knot in 1997 and share three children together. DeLeon Hayes celebrated the casting news on Instagram, writing: “Dream come true. Beyond honored to bring this story to life.”

Nate Dogg is Snoop Dogg’s older cousin who also grew up in Long Beach. They linked up for classics like “Ain’t No Fun (If the Homies Can’t Have None).” Nate Dogg died in 2011 at age 41.

The Lady of Rage was part of the Death Row Records family while Snoop Dogg was on the roster, and she appeared on Snoop’s Doggystyle debut.

Kurupt changed coasts, moving from Philly to California and became one of Death Row’s firs signees. He worked with Snoop during the early stages of his career and formed Tha Dogg Pound alongside Daz Dillinger. Sholotan starred as Carlton in the Bel-Air reboot.

While they were on opposing sides of the East Coast-West Coast beef, Biggie and Snoop remained allies. Snoop appeared on all three B.I.G. posthumous albums. SwayvoTwain, who is the son of D’Angelo and Angie Stone, is set to play Biggie.

RBX is actually Snoop Dogg’s cousin and both were part of the fabric making up Death Row during the label’s golden era. They teamed up as guests on “Stranded on Death Row” from Dr. Dre’s ‘The Chronic.’

Big Reecie Cup was the muscle protecting Snoop during his rise to stardom in Long Beach, and rapper G Perico is set to play the Crip gang member.

Wicked actress Cynthia Erivo is set to play 2Pac’s mother, Afeni Shakur. A fearless political activist, Afeni was a member of the Black Panther Party. Her worldview laid the blueprint for Pac to become a rap legend.

There’s nothing like that father-son connection. Master P signed Snoop Dogg to No Limit Records in 1998 and helped revive the Doggfather following his split from Death Row. Hercy Miller is stepping into acting after playing college basketball at a few schools, including the University of Louisville, and now will serve as the No Limit boss.

The D.O.C. was instrumental in helping Snoop Dogg develop as a songwriter and served as a mentor to Snoop since D.O.C. was also close with Dr. Dre after leaving Ruthless Records. Zachariah Rogers, a Tennessee native, is best known for playing Pico in P-Valley.

Tyquan Givens, who goes by Watts Homie Quan, has made a name for himself as a comedian and actor. Earlier this year, he appeared in the Snowfall spin-off The Drop and starred in the first season of The Vince Staples Show in 2024. Givens is slated to play an original character in the flick named B. Mack.

David Kenner served as Snoop Dogg’s lawyer on his highly publicized murder trial, in which Snoop was acquitted alongside his security guard in 1996. The two remained friends and Snoop even perfformed at Kenner’s 80th birthday party in 2021.

Jimmy Iovine’s Interscope Records partnered with Suge Knight’s Death Row Records, which turned Snoop into a star in the ’90s rap scene. Iovine was long a support of Snoop, comparing the rapper and Dr. Dre’s connection to the Rolling Stones’ Mick Jagger and Keith Richards.

#794. Canadian Government Introduces Canada Creative Credit to Support ‘Artistic Production’

The Mark Carney government's new federal budget also confirms a $600 million investment to provide relief to the audiovisual sector for 2026-27.

Canada has built a new support for the creative sector into the new federal budget.

The Carney government’s 2026 federal budget was tabled Thursday afternoon (Nov. 5), and it includes a new and forthcoming Canada Creative Credit, described as a tax relief “for Canadian artists to foster creativity, artistic production and cultural entrepreneurship.” In a subsequent message posted to X, prime minister Mark Carney revealed that Canadian artists can benefit from an exception of up to $45,000.

The new budget also confirms the government’s planned investment of $600 million into the audio and audiovisual sectors in Canada, which was originally announced in June as a means to provide “stability and immediate support” to the creative industry amid ongoing debates surrounding the CRTC’s CanCon regulations and the implementation of the Online Streaming Act. While the sum was described as an annual investment in the government’s initial news release, the current budget only lists the amount for 2026-27 fiscal year.

Several Canadian music organizations have welcomed the news, including SaskMusic, the East Coast Music Association and the Canadian Live Music Association (CLMA), who says it “looks forward to working with partners across government and cultural sectors to ensure investment in live music activity in Canada.” Adisq, the Québec Association for the Recording, Concert and Video, highlighted the temporary nature of the investment and the need for “stable, foreseeable financial resources” that can adequately meet the challenges companies are faced with, but also shared a positive reaction.

“The local music industry operates in a challenging economic and technological environment where our music struggles to reach its audiences. By following through on its June commitment, the government will provide tangible support to our sector,” says Eve Paré, executive director of Adisq.

Canada stepped in to announce the $600 million investment after the CRTC announced its intention to triple the base contribution that major streamers and Canadian broadcasters who make over $25 million in annual revenue must pay to fund the creation Canadian content, raising it from 5 to 15%.

While some Canadian music organizations and associations like FACTOR and Music Canada applauded the government for providing a financial boost to the sector, others such as the Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists (ACTRA) criticized it for potentially letting foreign streaming platforms off the hook. Nonetheless, the CRTC doubled down on its plans to implement its CanCon regulations in August after trade talks between the U.S. and Canada fell through.

“It is essential that the CRTC have the full discretion needed to establish a fair framework in which all stakeholders in the system—whether traditional or digital—contribute their fair share to local culture. They must help fund it and ensure its discoverability. This is the prerequisite for establishing a sustainable broadcasting system that effectively supports our music,” Paré adds.

The 2026-27 federal budget is offering direct support to Canadian broadcasting by offering an additional $300 million in funding for CBC/Radio-Canada, which will be allocated over two years. As Canada gears up to celebrate its 160th birthday, the country is also looking to provide an additional $10M to the Building Communities through Arts and Heritage (BCAH) program, which provides funding to local festivals, among other initiatives. Ottawa Bluesfest is one of 20 festivals nationwide highlighted in the budget that received funding from the program last year and poised to receive additional funding for 2027-28, per the budget. While Festivals and Major Events Canada (FAME) acknowledges the boost, it says it is “too temporary to have the transformative impact the sector has been seeking.”

The government is also allocating $393.2 million over three years to “advance Canada’s Francophonie leadership objectives” as it gears up to host the Francophonie Summit in Ottawa-Gatineau in 2028. Adisq salutes the government’s investment, saying that French-language music “will be present.”

This story was originally published by Billboard Canada.

#793. Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins

An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.

The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.

The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.

A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle

For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.

That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.

The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.

"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.

The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.

An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth

The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.

The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.

Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.

The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.

Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.

"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.

As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.

A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree

The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.

Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.

To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.

The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.

By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.

The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.

Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?

Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.

That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.

Geography may help explain why this region was so important.

Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.

Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.

Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.

The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.

Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.

Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived

The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.

Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.

"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."

Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.

The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.

The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.

More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt

Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.

Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.

The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.

For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.

A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.

Hoda Kotb is glad her ex Joel Schiffman will be there for their daughters today—and everyday.

The Today show alum to came a revelation about her co-parenting dynamic with the businessman—who she split from in 2022 following eight years of dating—after the two recently reunited to watch their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, take part in their school's Halloween parade.

“Usually, my kids wave and try to hide," Kotb shared as she filled in for Sheinelle Jones on the Nov. 9 episode of Today With Jenna & Sheinelle, adding that time time, "They saw Joel at the fence and beelined. They were saying to their friends, ‘That’s my dad,’ because they don't see him as much.”

For the 62-year-old, that exchange became a "very meaningful" moment in her motherhood journey as she realized the value in encouraging him to come more.

"As the girls are getting older, having their dad there is much more important than ever," Kotb explained. "When I was watching them say that, I thought, 'Oh my gosh, come all the time, be here as often as you can, because it matters.'"

#791. James Gunn and Peter Safran Leaving as DC Studios’ Co-CEOS

Four years after taking up the mantle as the head of DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran announced they are stepping down at the end of November.

It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s yet another shakeup at DC Studios!

Four years after James Gunn and Peter Safran were announced as the new heads of DC Studios—overseeing the line up of DC films, TV and animation—the dynamic duo announced they are stepping down at the end of November following the purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery by Skydance. They will be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham.

“Oh, boy. What a four years,” Gunn posted to Instagram Nov. 9. “Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios.”

The Superman director shared it was “a dream come true” to oversee DC’s super-powered slate of characters like Superman, Batman and Supergirl, saying it was truly a “unique opportunity” he couldn’t say no to.

Of course, with the “highest of the highs”—like directing the upcoming Man of Tomorrow and working alongside Safran—the 60-year-old also revealed that only those closest to him know that the past four years have also “been trying, to say the least.”

“I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that),” he added. “I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and l've stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.”

Gunn also had a special note for the wonder woman in his life, wife Jennifer Holland, writing, “Jenn, I love you and I'm sorry and you don't need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I'm no longer doing this job.”

And while he will “miss the people around” him and the heroes he got to be “co-caretaker” of, he is ready to release a new issue of his career and “get back to pure filmmaking.”

Still, saying goodbye to DC Studios does not mean ending the run of his upcoming projects, as he clarified that he is still working on a secret DC project in addition to Man of Tomorrow and producing Batman: Part II and the TV series The People v. Gorilla Grodd.

As for Latcham, who is taking up the mantle from Gunn and Safran—who themselves took over for previous DC head Walter Hamada—he has a history in the comics world, serving as producer on Iron-Man, The Avengers and Guardians of the Galaxy, which Gunn directed before being fired by Marvel over past offensive tweets.

“The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility,” Latcham shared in a Nov. 9 press release, “that I do not take lightly.”

And Gunn and Safran were thrilled Latcham answered the Bat-signal, adding in the release, “We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”

#790. The Nightmare Before Christmas: Michael Jackson, Wham! & Mariah Carey Hits Celebrate Dual Holidays on the Hot 100

Five Halloween classics, one newer paranormal-themed pop hit & two Christmas carols scale the chart.

The Billboard Hot 100 is decorated with both spiderwebs and mistletoe, thanks to hits central to Halloween and Christmas.

As previously reported, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” hunts down a new No. 2 Hot 100 peak, more than 42 years after it first made the chart. It previously peaked at No. 4 in March 1984.

Five Halloween classics — plus Tame Impala and JENNIE’s modern entry into the creepy song canon, “Dracula” — and two Christmas favorites scale the Nov. 14-dated Hot 100, which reflects data in the United States Oct. 30-Nov. 5, according to Luminate. The tracking week, thus, encompassed Halloween and, the following day, Mariah Carey’s annual proclamation that once again it’s ti-ime for the yuletide season.

Here’s a rundown of the Halloween and Christmas-themed songs on the latest Hot 100 and their chart-eligible streams and week-over-week gains.

17.4 million streams (up 87%)The song, released on the late King of Pop’s Thriller, also drew 11.3 million in radio airplay audience (up 172%) and sold 4,000 (up 48%).

11 million streams (up 87%)The theme to the blockbuster movie of the same name was No. 1 on the Hot 100 for three weeks in 1984. Parker Jr. has his highest placement since the song wrapped its run in the top 10 that September.

9.8 million streams (up 60%)The Danny Elfman-written song, which surpasses its previous No. 26 high set last year, is from 1993’s animated hit movie The Nightmare Before Christmas (which mirrors the mix of Halloween- and Christmas-themed music on the chart).

7.4 million streams (up 228%)Andrew Ridgeley and the late George Michael’s chestnut, from 1984, takes the early lead among winter holiday hits. It rose to a new No. 2 best last holiday season.

#788. Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease

A pesticide used for decades in agriculture may be linked to a much greater risk of Parkinson's disease, and scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for how it damages the brain.

Researchers at UCLA Health found that people with long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos, a widely used pesticide, had more than 2.5 times the risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared with those who were not exposed. Laboratory experiments also revealed how the chemical can interfere with the brain's ability to remove damaged proteins, leading to the loss of nerve cells essential for controlling movement.

The study, published in Molecular Neurodegeneration, goes beyond identifying a connection between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's. By examining what happens inside affected brain cells, the researchers uncovered a biological mechanism that could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain from damage.

A Common Pesticide With a Troubling Link to Parkinson's

Parkinson's disease affects nearly one million Americans. The progressive neurological condition gradually damages brain cells involved in movement, often causing tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with coordination.

One of the defining features of Parkinson's is the loss of neurons that produce dopamine. This chemical messenger allows nerve cells to communicate and helps the brain coordinate smooth, controlled movements. As dopamine levels decline, the brain becomes less capable of regulating those movements.

Although inherited genetic factors can influence who develops Parkinson's, researchers have increasingly focused on environmental exposures that may also contribute to the disease. Pesticides are of particular interest because some chemicals used to kill insects or other agricultural pests can also interfere with biological processes in the nervous system.

Chlorpyrifos has been used extensively in agriculture for decades. Its residential use was banned in the United States in 2001, and agricultural applications faced additional restrictions in 2021. However, the pesticide remains in use on many crops in the United States and continues to be widely applied in other countries.

Because exposure may have occurred years before symptoms appeared, understanding the potential long-term effects of chlorpyrifos is particularly important. Identifying specific chemicals associated with Parkinson's could help researchers develop prevention strategies and determine whether previously exposed individuals might benefit from additional neurological monitoring.

Researchers Find More Than Double the Parkinson's Risk

To investigate the connection, UCLA scientists examined information from 829 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and 824 people without the condition. All participants were enrolled in the university's long-running Parkinson's Environment and Genes study, which investigates how environmental exposures and inherited factors influence Parkinson's risk.

The researchers combined California's detailed pesticide application records with participants' residential and workplace address histories. This allowed them to estimate how much chlorpyrifos individuals may have encountered over time based on where they lived and worked.

The results revealed a striking association. People with prolonged residential exposure to chlorpyrifos had more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease compared with those who had no such exposure.

Although this population analysis could not establish that the pesticide directly caused Parkinson's, the researchers took an additional step to investigate whether chlorpyrifos could produce the kinds of brain damage seen in people with the disease.

The team exposed mice to chlorpyrifos in aerosol form for 11 weeks. The inhalation approach was designed to resemble a common way people may encounter pesticides in the environment.

The exposed mice developed movement difficulties and lost neurons responsible for producing dopamine. This was particularly significant because the degeneration of these same nerve cells is a central feature of Parkinson's disease.

The researchers also detected inflammation in the animals' brains, along with abnormal accumulations of a protein called alpha-synuclein.

Under normal conditions, alpha-synuclein is found in nerve cells and plays a role in their functioning. However, the protein can accumulate in abnormal clumps that are closely associated with Parkinson's disease. These deposits are a major focus of research into why certain brain cells gradually deteriorate.

Together, the findings showed that chlorpyrifos exposure could reproduce several important characteristics of Parkinson's in laboratory animals, strengthening the biological evidence behind the human population findings.

Scientists Uncover a Breakdown in the Brain's Cleanup System

The researchers then turned to zebrafish to investigate exactly how chlorpyrifos harms neurons. These small fish are frequently used in neuroscience research because they allow scientists to study biological processes involved in nerve cell development and survival.

Their experiments pointed to a disruption in autophagy, a natural cellular maintenance process that helps remove damaged proteins and other unwanted material.

Autophagy functions much like an internal recycling system. Cells use it to break down worn-out or defective components so that potentially harmful material does not accumulate. This process is especially important for neurons, many of which must remain functional throughout a person's lifetime.

When chlorpyrifos interfered with this cleanup system, damaged material accumulated inside neurons, contributing to their deterioration.

The researchers also made an encouraging discovery. When they restored the cellular cleanup process or removed synuclein protein in their experiments, the neurons were protected from damage.

This finding suggests that the pesticide's harmful effects may depend partly on a biological pathway that researchers could potentially target with future treatments.

A Potential New Strategy for Protecting Against Parkinson's

The discovery raises the possibility of developing therapies that strengthen the brain's cellular cleanup mechanisms and help protect vulnerable neurons. Such treatments might eventually prove useful for people exposed to chlorpyrifos or other pesticides that disrupt similar processes.

However, the protective effects have so far been demonstrated in laboratory models. Additional research will be needed to determine whether enhancing autophagy can prevent or reduce pesticide-related brain damage in humans.

Scientists also want to investigate whether other commonly used pesticides interfere with the same cellular mechanisms. Although chlorpyrifos use has declined in the United States, many people were exposed before restrictions were introduced, and related agricultural chemicals remain widely used.

The findings could also help identify people with a history of substantial pesticide exposure who may benefit from closer neurological monitoring. Earlier recognition of possible changes in brain function could become increasingly important as researchers work toward treatments that slow or prevent Parkinson's progression.

Dr. Jeff Bronstein, professor of Neurology at UCLA Health and the study's senior author, emphasized the importance of identifying a particular chemical rather than treating all pesticides as a single category.

"This study establishes chlorpyrifos as a specific environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, not just pesticides as a general class," said Dr. Jeff Bronstein.

"By showing the biological mechanism in animal models, we've demonstrated that this association is likely causal. The discovery that autophagy dysfunction drives the neurotoxicity also points us toward potential therapeutic strategies to protect vulnerable brain cells."

#785. U2 Celebrate Brian Eno With Secret Show at London’s Tate Museum: Best Moments

The band release their 16th studio album Carnaval de Luze next Friday (Nov. 13).

Speaking on the New York Times’ Interview podcast, U2’s Bono discussed some of the advice that they’ve heeded from Sulinna Ong – newly appointed to the band’s management team alongside Irving and Jeffrey Azoff – on how to cut through in this fragmented era of culture and music: show up in unexpected places. That seemingly began in September with a return to their old school, 50 years on from their formation, and popped up again on Grafton Street in Dublin for a surprise free show.

Before U2 tackles the NFL’s Thanksgiving halftime show later this month – following 2025’s appearance by Beyoncé – the band continued its surprising streak with a secret show at London’s Tate Modern Museum on Tuesday (Nov. 3). The location was only revealed to fans hours before the show began, with entry only possible via a ballot win.

Even then came another twist: the band would not be gracing the Turbine Hall, where performers such as PJ Harvey and Kraftwerk have filled the cavernous room with their songs. Instead, the quartet played inside The Tanks, a claustrophobic, brutalist 400-capacity cave underneath the Blavatnik Building usually reserved for experiential exhibitions. There were no giant LED screens or mobile phones, which were locked away in pouches – unlike any U2 concert in recent memory, then. A half-century in, there’s still a trick or two up the band’s sleeve.

The show was recorded for the BBC and will be broadcast on television and its streaming service iPlayer later this month. The flurry of activity comes amidst a major return for the rock titans, as they release 16th studio album Carnaval de Luze (Nov. 13) and gear up for a globetrotting tour that’ll kick off in 2027 and roll into 2028. This show and the upcoming tour features all four members, with Larry Mullen Jr. rejoining Bono, The Edge and Adam Clayton after missing the 2023-24 Sphere residency following neck surgery.

The night saw greatest hits, new songs, frequent tributes to longtime comrade Brian Eno and the odd soliloquy from Bono regarding the special setting and their connection to the arts. These were the five best moments.

Playfully called the “fish tank” by Bono, the concrete structure appeared fairly unassuming as lucky punters and industry bigwigs – including Noel Gallagher and Lily Allen – filtered into the seated venue; Fine art students, invited from local colleges and schools, lounged on beanbags at the foot of the stage. The room’s bare walls were brought to life by Brian Eno, a close collaborator integral to the band’s story, who produced their best-selling LPs The Joshua Tree (1987) and Achtung Baby (1991), among others.

Eno’s impressionistic work 77 Million Paintings was projected onto the walls, filling the room with an ever-changing backdrop of soft, vibrant colours and playful squiggles. Developed in 2006, the generative software randomly combines different shades and shapes to create something completely unique with every transition. “We’re here to celebrate the work of Brian tonight,” Bono said, frequently returning to acknowledge an irreplaceable collaborator; each of the songs performed on the night was produced by Eno.

U2 has a number of undroppable songs on its usual setlist — take your pick! — but “Bad” had surprisingly been absent from the band’s sets since 2019; the brooding epic did not feature in the band’s celebrated Sphere residency in Las Vegas. But when it arrived as this show’s second song and sounded just as impassioned as it does in the biggest venues, though Bono’s usual post-chorus yelps of “I’m wide awake” are now sung with a greater clarity and purpose.

Given the unique setting, Bono took the opportunity to discuss relatively unheard stories, particularly their connection to the art world. He referenced the late French-American artist Louise Bourgeois, whose Maman – a 30ft bronze spider sculpture – christened the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall upon its opening in 2000. Clayton, Bono said, purchased his first work by Bourgeois in the 1990s, and the frontman once sang “Amazing Grace” for her in her apartment, “despite not knowing the second verse.” He improvised, he said, and did the same during this performance, creating a makeshift trumpet out of his hands, reflecting on how art can inspire creation even when the words won’t come.

Carnaval de Luze arrives amidst something of a creative purple patch for the band, following the release of the Days of Ash and Easter Lily EPs earlier this spring. Original material in the past two decades has been left wanting, but two unreleased tracks – “Can’t Stop Us Now” and “The Greatest Show on Earth” – held their own in a setlist that included “Beautiful Day,” “Pride (In the Name of Love),” “One,” and more classics. The latter in particular skilfully brings together each individual element – The Edge’s airy guitar, Clayton’s driving bass, and the punchy beat of Mullen Jr. – in one of the quartet’s most impactful songs in years. They’re delivered with supreme confidence, too, a recognition that U2 is in such a strong position right now.

Prior to “In a Little While,” Bono revealed that the song’s origins came from a drinking session featuring Spanish wine recommended by Eno – which, he claimed, has a particular inspiration for painters. The resulting song, which features on 2000’s All That You Can’t Leave Behind, was written on a mighty hangover, Bono explained, hence its hushed, reverent tone.

Eno loomed large in the evening, with each song played in the 11-song setlist produced or written alongside him. During the closing song “With or Without You,” Bono prowled the room searching for Eno, bringing him on stage for a round of applause during the song’s soaring crescendo.

#784. 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought

More than 30,000 years ago, people living across Ice Age Europe were far more connected than scientists previously believed. New genetic evidence reveals unexpected links between populations separated by enormous distances, challenging the long-held idea that eastern and western European groups remained largely isolated from one another.

An international research team led by the University of Vienna made the discovery by analyzing ancient DNA from rare human remains and traces of human genetic material preserved in cave sediments. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide a new picture of how prehistoric Europeans interacted, exchanged genes, and maintained populations through thousands of years of dramatic environmental change.

The research focuses on people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian), which flourished across the continent roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. Archaeological discoveries have long suggested that these ancient populations maintained connections over considerable distances. However, previous genetic evidence pointed to relatively distinct eastern and western ancestry groups.

By combining new genetic findings with previously collected DNA, researchers uncovered evidence that these groups were more interconnected than expected. They also found signs that certain populations in southwestern Europe maintained their genetic ancestry for thousands of years.

A Woman From 30,000 Years Ago Reveals Hidden Genetic Connections

One of the most revealing discoveries came from the remains of a woman who lived approximately 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France. Found at Isturitz Cave, her remains provided the oldest genome-wide genetic dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Her DNA contained a surprising combination of ancestry. Although most of her genetic background was associated with western European populations, she also carried ancestry linked to people from central and eastern Europe.

Using genetic modeling, researchers estimated that this mixing between populations occurred approximately 32,500 to 31,500 years ago. The finding suggests that genetic connections extended across large portions of Europe much earlier than scientists had previously established.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. "Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected."

The researchers identified a similar genetic signature in another ancient individual whose remains had previously been studied at Ormesson, France. Combined with archaeological discoveries, the evidence strengthens the possibility that Isturitz Cave served as a gathering place where different groups of prehistoric people encountered one another.

Ancient DNA Hidden in Cave Sediments Reveals Ice Age Survival

While some ancient Europeans exchanged genes across considerable distances, other populations appear to have maintained a continuous genetic presence in particular regions for thousands of years.

Evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain suggests that ancestry associated with western European populations persisted in southwestern Europe over an extended period.

The researchers also used an increasingly valuable technique that allows scientists to recover human DNA directly from cave sediments, even when no identifiable human remains are present. Tiny traces of genetic material left behind by ancient inhabitants can survive in soil and other deposits for thousands of years, providing information about people whose bones have never been found.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, Spain, the team recovered human nuclear DNA from a sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years. Despite finding no human bones or teeth in the layer, they obtained enough genetic information to determine the ancestry of the people who had occupied the site.

"Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing," says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. "This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site."

The results indicate that western European ancestry persisted in the region through the Last Glacial Maximum, a period when enormous ice sheets reached their greatest extent during the last Ice Age.

This supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula, which includes present-day Spain and Portugal, served as an important refuge for prehistoric humans during some of the coldest conditions of the Ice Age.

Ancient Mother and Son Offer Clues About Prehistoric Mating

Another revealing discovery came from southern Italy, where researchers examined the genetic remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus believed to be the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1.

Genetic analysis suggests that the child's father likely belonged to the same ancestral population as his mother. However, the parents were not closely related, offering evidence that mating patterns within these ancient communities may have helped limit inbreeding.

This finding adds another dimension to the emerging picture of prehistoric European societies. Even as some populations maintained relatively stable genetic ancestry within their home regions, they could also participate in broader networks of genetic exchange spanning considerable distances.

Together, the discoveries show that long-term regional continuity and widespread genetic connections were not mutually exclusive. Both helped shape the population history of Ice Age Europe.

Building on these results, Gelabert and his colleagues are now combining DNA recovered from ancient sediments with advanced proteomic techniques, which examine proteins for clues about past life. Their goal is to investigate the earliest expansions of modern humans across Europe, including how these populations interacted with carnivores in places where bones and other organic remains are scarce.

Materials provided by University of Vienna. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#783. Pink’s Major Career Move Will Just Give You a Reason to Celebrate

Pink announced she is taking her acrobatics and tracklist to a new Las Vegas residency at The Sphere, making her the first female solo artist to have a residency at the venue.

Pink is soaring to new heights—and a new milestone.

The “So What!” singer announced her first-ever residency will kick off next year at The Sphere in Las Vegas, making her the first female solo artist to headline a residency at the venue.

“Makes me think of celebration. Makes me feel like I’m on top of the world,” Pink wrote on Instagram Nov. 9. “This idea has been bubbling up for years. And I finally get to share it with all of you! Let’s celebrate!”

The 47-year-old also noted her residency—nine shows across September and October—will commemorate “the highs, the lows, the new” and “the scary” of her career while alluding that the concert may also feature some acts that have “never been done before.”

While Pink may be flipping out about her new show, she’s had much to celebrate this year. After all, her chart-topping album Missundaztood, featuring hits like “Don’t Let Me Get Me” and “Just Like a Pill,” turned 25 last month.

“Twenty-effing-five years. Can you believe it?” she shared on Instagram Oct. 16. “You’ve been screaming this song louder than me since 2001, and I’ll never get sick of it. Thank you for showing up to this party every single time.”

Plus, Pink somersaulted her way into hosting the 2026 Tony Awards in June—an ace landing for her and husband Carey Hart’s 15-year-old daughter Willow, who has been vocal about her love for theater.

“There has been so much love pouring in, and I’m overwhelmed by gratitude,” the Grammy winner wrote on Instagram after the awards show. “My favorite thing about my life is the collaboration that ensues.”

Pink's athleticism was put to the ultimate test at the 2012 AMAs, and boy did she pass with flying colors. Singing "Try," the musician was joined by a male dance partner who at one point lifted Pink above his shoulders as she hit the splits.

Pink received a standing ovation for her performance of "Try" during Music's Biggest Night in 2014. The Cirque du Soleil-inspired piece concluded with an outfit change as she took the stage alongside Nate Reuss for "Just Give Me a Reason.

Pink took her Cirque de Soleil-inspired routine to new heights (literally) when she belted out "Beautiful Trauma" on the exterior of the JW Marriott hotel in downtown Los Angeles.

The pop star let her amazing vocals do all the talking when she took the Grammys stage dressed simply in oversized denim and a white T-shirt. A sign language interpreter performed "Wild Hearts Can't Broken" alongside Pink.
